It is not a general list of every table that happens to contain a field with similar wording. For example, an Employee ID Number field owned by EMPLOYEES may also appear in PART-TIME EMPLOYEES and FULL-TIME EMPLOYEES subset tables. Those related tables can be listed under Shared By because the field participates in their explicit relationships. This element helps document where the field is used while preserving clarity about its parent table and role in the design.

Study instruction:
- Draw a parent table with related subset tables and complete the Shared By element only for the tables connected through explicit relationships.

Key point:
- Shared By records relationship-based sharing, not casual similarity between fields.
- The parent table remains the field’s owning table.
15. Q: What is a field alias, and when may an alias be necessary?
A: Show answer
An alias is an alternative name used for a field in a limited set of circumstances. The chapter illustrates a case where the same Employee ID Number field is needed twice in one SUBSIDIARIES table: once to identify the president and once to identify the vice president. Since the database structure should not contain two indistinguishable occurrences of the same field name, aliases such as President ID Number and Vice President ID Number can distinguish the two roles. The underlying field meaning remains based on the employee identifier, while the alias clarifies the specific role for that occurrence. Aliases should be used sparingly because excessive use makes definitions harder to maintain and can obscure the original meaning.

Study instruction:
- Analyze a table that needs the same employee reference in two role-based positions and propose aliases that clarify each occurrence without changing the field’s underlying meaning.

Key point:
- Aliases distinguish exceptional multiple occurrences of the same field in one table.
- Excessive aliases can conceal meaning and complicate maintenance.
16. Q: What risks arise when aliases are used too freely?
A: Show answer
Too many aliases can make the database difficult to manage because a single underlying field may appear to have several unrelated identities. Users and designers may lose sight of what the original field represents, and future relationship work may become confusing. An alias should solve a real naming collision or role-distinction problem, not serve as a convenient way to rename fields informally. The designer should retain the standard Field Name and record aliases only where the structure requires distinct occurrences or role-specific references. Each alias should have a clear business reason and be understandable to the people who maintain and use the data dictionary.

Study instruction:
- Review proposed aliases and remove those that merely duplicate familiar terminology or obscure the standard field identity.

Key point:
- Aliases should be exceptional and purpose-driven.
- Preserve the connection between an alias and the field’s authoritative definition.
17. Q: What is the purpose of the Description element in a field specification?
A: Show answer
Description provides a complete interpretation of the field. It explains what the field represents, its purpose, and its role within the table or in relation to the table’s subject. Writing the description forces the designer and the organization to think carefully about the nature of the data being stored. If the field’s meaning cannot be described clearly, that may indicate that the field itself needs refinement. A strong description supplements the field name rather than merely repeating it, and it should be understandable to users throughout the organization rather than only to technical staff.

Study instruction:
- Write a full description for a field and test whether a user unfamiliar with the database can identify the meaning and organizational purpose without relying on the field name alone.

Key point:
- A description gives a field a clear interpretation and purpose.
- Difficulty describing a field can reveal an unresolved definition or design problem.
18. Q: What makes a field description accurate and useful?
A: Show answer
A useful description accurately identifies the field and clearly states what it represents. It should explain the field’s purpose and how it relates to the subject of its parent table. For example, a customer city field might be defined as the metropolitan area in which a customer resides or conducts business and as an integral part of the customer’s address. This is more informative than saying simply that it is a customer’s city. The description should be complete enough to avoid ambiguity but concise enough to be read and understood easily. It should provide meaning that the field name alone cannot convey.

Study instruction:
- Improve a vague field definition by adding the business meaning, purpose, and relationship to the parent subject.

Key point:
- Define both what the value represents and why it is part of the table.
- Do not settle for circular wording that simply expands the field name.
19. Q: Why should a field description avoid merely restating the field name?
A: Show answer
Rephrasing the field name adds no meaningful information about the field’s purpose. A description such as “CustLast Name—the last name of a customer” tells the reader little more than the name itself. A stronger description explains what counts as the customer’s surname and how the organization uses it, such as for formal communication and correspondence. The objective is to remove ambiguity, not to create a longer version of the label. A reviewer should be able to learn something about the data’s intended meaning and business context from the description that is not already obvious from the field name.

Study instruction:
- Rewrite descriptions that simply restate their field names, adding a meaningful explanation of scope, purpose, or use.

Key point:
- Descriptions should add interpretation rather than repeat labels.
- Useful wording clarifies the value’s meaning in its business context.
20. Q: Why should field descriptions avoid technical jargon, acronyms, and abbreviations?
A: Show answer
A field description is intended to communicate the field’s meaning to anyone who needs to understand the data, including users and managers who may not know specialized terminology. An unexplained acronym can make an otherwise simple definition unintelligible. Rather than assuming that every reader knows an internal code or technical phrase, the designer should use plain language and describe the field’s purpose directly. If a specialized term is essential, it should be explained clearly. The description should be accessible across the organization and should not depend on knowledge held by one department or technical team.

Study instruction:
- Review a set of field descriptions and replace unexplained acronyms or technical jargon with plain language understood by nontechnical users.

Key point:
- Field descriptions are organizational documentation, not developer-only notes.
- Use clear language and explain unavoidable specialized terms.
21. Q: Why should a field description exclude implementation-specific information?
A: Show answer
A field description should define the data’s meaning, not the screen, menu, program, or code in which it appears. Implementation details may change when the database application or user interface is updated, while the business meaning of the field may remain constant. Including interface-specific references would make the data dictionary less durable and could cause readers to confuse a field’s purpose with the way it is currently accessed. Details about screens, forms, reports, and program logic belong in implementation documentation. The logical field description should remain relevant regardless of the particular RDBMS or application used to store and display the data.

Study instruction:
- Remove references to screens, menus, application modules, and code from sample descriptions and identify the appropriate implementation documentation for those details.

Key point:
- Logical descriptions explain the field’s meaning, not its current user-interface location.
- Keep implementation details separate so the data dictionary remains stable.
22. Q: Why should field descriptions be independent of other field descriptions?
A: Show answer
Each description should be sufficiently complete to explain its own field without requiring the reader to look up another field’s definition. Cross-references such as “see Quantity On Hand” may leave the meaning unclear when the description is viewed separately and can create unnecessary dependencies in the data dictionary. The designer should state the field’s meaning and purpose directly. Where two fields are related, that relationship can be explained in the appropriate model or documentation, but it should not be necessary to consult one description to understand another. Independent descriptions are easier to review, update, and reuse.

Study instruction:
- Identify cross-dependent descriptions and rewrite them so that each field can be understood on its own.

Key point:
- Every field description should stand on its own.
- Model relationships explicitly rather than relying on cross-references in definitions.
23. Q: Why should field descriptions avoid examples?
A: Show answer
An example can illustrate one possible value but may not define the full range or meaning of the field. A description that depends on examples can become incomplete or require several additional examples to cover the subject properly. The chapter recommends a direct, concise definition that explains the field without relying on illustrative cases. Examples can still be used in training material or separate guidance where they help users understand how to enter data, but the core field description should remain a self-contained definition. This keeps the specification clear and avoids confusion between examples and mandatory business rules.

Study instruction:
- Rewrite a field description that lists sample values so that it defines the complete meaning without relying on examples.

Key point:
- Examples are useful for training but should not replace a complete field definition.
- Keep the formal Description concise, complete, and self-explanatory.
24. Q: What do Physical Elements describe in a field specification?
A: Show answer
Physical Elements describe the general structure of the data held by a field. The chapter uses Data Type, Length, Decimal Places, and Character Support. These elements are intentionally expressed in general terms because different RDBMS applications may offer different specific data types and implementation options. Defining them during logical design gives the organization a consistent view of the field’s intended structure and reduces the effort needed when the database is implemented. These settings should be chosen according to the actual nature of the data, not simply because one particular database application offers a convenient default.

Study instruction:
- Complete the Physical Elements for several different fields and explain how each setting reflects the field’s intended data values.

Key point:
- Physical Elements govern the structure and permitted format of stored values.
- The logical specification should be clear even though implementation details vary by RDBMS.
25. Q: What data types does the chapter use for logical field specification?
A: Show answer
The chapter uses three general data types: Alphanumeric, Numeric, and DateTime. Alphanumeric stores combinations of letters, numbers, keyboard characters, and special characters. Numeric stores whole and real numbers and is not intended for values whose leading zeroes are significant identifiers. DateTime stores dates, times, or a combination of the two. These are deliberately broad categories for the logical design stage; an RDBMS may provide a wider and more specific set of data types during implementation. The designer should identify the nature of the information first and then select the appropriate technical type in the target platform later.

Study instruction:
- Assign one of the three general data types to a set of fields and explain why the choice matches the meaning and format of each value.

Key point:
- Alphanumeric, Numeric, and DateTime are the chapter’s broad logical data types.
- Numeric values should not be used when leading zeroes are significant parts of an identifier.
26. Q: When should an identifier be stored as Alphanumeric rather than Numeric?
A: Show answer
Use Alphanumeric when the value may contain letters, combinations of characters, or leading zeroes that are significant to the identifier. The chapter notes that Numeric does not accept leading zeroes as part of a genuine number because those zeroes do not change the numeric value. An employee or product code such as 000234 may therefore need an Alphanumeric representation if the exact formatting is part of the identifier. If the field stores a quantity or amount used in arithmetic, Numeric is more appropriate. The decision should be based on whether the value represents a mathematical quantity or a coded label whose character sequence must be preserved.

Study instruction:
- Classify sample values as quantities or identifiers and decide whether Numeric or Alphanumeric preserves their intended meaning.

Key point:
- Numeric is for numbers used as numeric values; Alphanumeric can preserve meaningful formatting and leading zeroes.
- Choose the type based on semantics, not merely whether the value looks like digits.
27. Q: What does the Length element specify?
A: Show answer
Length specifies the total number of characters a user can enter for a field value. It helps define the expected size of the stored value and can prevent excessively long or incomplete data. The maximum that can be implemented depends on the RDBMS, and some applications handle numeric field lengths through specific numeric types rather than a user-defined character length. The designer should select a length that accommodates valid values without being unnecessarily broad. The setting should reflect the business data requirement, while the implementation team maps the logical specification to the capabilities of the chosen RDBMS.

Study instruction:
- Determine reasonable lengths for a range of identifiers, names, descriptions, and postal attributes, explaining the business evidence supporting each choice.

Key point:
- Length sets the permitted size of a field value.
- Actual implementation limits depend on the selected RDBMS and data type.
28. Q: What does Decimal Places control?
A: Show answer
Decimal Places records how many digits are permitted to the right of the decimal point in a real-number value. It determines the precision represented by the field. For example, an organization may need a particular level of precision for prices or other amounts, depending on the meaning of the value and its business requirements. A field that stores whole counts may need zero decimal places, while a field intended to store fractional measurements or monetary amounts may require more. The chapter’s example of currency precision illustrates that the required number of decimal places should be established from the organization’s needs rather than selected arbitrarily.

Study instruction:
- Review numeric fields in a sample system and specify the appropriate decimal precision based on the measurement or business meaning of each field.

Key point:
- Decimal Places determines the precision to the right of the decimal point.
- Set precision according to the field’s actual purpose and requirements.
29. Q: What is Character Support, and why is it needed in addition to Data Type?
A: Show answer
Character Support specifies which categories of characters users may enter into a field. An Alphanumeric data type permits a broad mix of letters, numbers, keyboard characters, and special characters, but not all of those characters make sense for every field. For example, a state abbreviation field should accept letters but not arbitrary punctuation or symbols. Character Support narrows the allowed character categories so that the data type does not permit meaningless entries. It is a field-level control that complements, rather than replaces, the broader data-type definition.

Study instruction:
- For a state field, product code, and free-text description, specify which character categories should be allowed and explain why they differ.

Key point:
- Data Type describes the broad data format; Character Support restricts character categories.
- Restrict entry to characters that make sense for the field’s purpose.
30. Q: Which character categories can be controlled through Character Support?
A: Show answer
The chapter identifies Letters, Numbers, Keyboard characters, and Special characters. Letters include alphabetic characters and examples from other languages, such as accented letters. Numbers are digits zero through nine. Keyboard characters are standard symbols and punctuation that are not letters or numbers, such as commas, slashes, parentheses, and percent signs. Special characters include symbols that may require key combinations or special software, such as copyright, trademark, and mathematical symbols. The designer can include or exclude these categories according to the field’s intended content. The setting should be tailored rather than allowing every possible character in every field.

Study instruction:
- Build a character-support matrix for common field types and justify whether letters, digits, keyboard punctuation, and special symbols should be accepted.

Key point:
- Character Support controls four broad categories of input characters.
- The permitted set should match the field’s meaning and expected values.
31. Q: What do Logical Elements govern in a field specification?
A: Show answer
Logical Elements govern the field’s role in the database and the rules that apply to its values. The chapter lists Key Type, Key Structure, Uniqueness, Null Support, Values Entered By, Required Value, Range of Values, and Edit Rule. These elements determine whether the field is a primary, alternate, foreign, or non-key; whether a key is simple or composite; whether values can repeat or be absent; who supplies the value; whether entry is mandatory; which values are valid; and whether the value may be changed. Logical Elements turn the specification into practical rules that support field-level integrity and consistent data handling.

Study instruction:
- Explain the control question answered by each Logical Element and apply each one to a sample field.

Key point:
- Logical Elements govern a field’s role, value validity, completeness, and changeability.
- They provide the value-level rules needed to enforce field-level integrity.
32. Q: What does the Key Type element record?
A: Show answer
Key Type identifies the field’s role in the table: non-key, primary key, alternate key, or foreign key. The chapter explains that the designer has already identified primary and alternate keys in the preceding stage, while foreign-key designation is completed when table relationships are established later. A non-key is a descriptive field that does not serve as one of these identifiers or relationship fields. The setting should reflect the role established in the logical model rather than a guess based on the field name. Proper classification helps determine which other logical settings, such as uniqueness and Null support, are appropriate.

Study instruction:
- Review a table structure with its keys already identified and complete the Key Type setting for each field, noting which foreign-key decisions await relationship design.

Key point:
- Key Type records the structural role of the field.
- Foreign-key status is assigned in the relationship-design stage described later in the book.
33. Q: What does the Key Structure element specify?
A: Show answer
Key Structure identifies whether a primary key is simple, consisting of one field, or composite, consisting of multiple fields. It applies to a field designated as part of a primary key. The element helps clarify how the key should be understood and implemented when the table’s identity depends on one or several fields. A composite key must be considered as one complete identifying combination; its individual components should not be mistaken for separate primary keys. Clear documentation of the key structure is important when later relationship work must use the appropriate identifier or field combination.

Study instruction:
- Identify simple and composite primary keys in a sample schema and record the Key Structure setting for each key.

Key point:
- Simple means one field; composite means multiple fields acting together.
- The full composite key is one identifier, not several independent primary keys.
34. Q: How should the Uniqueness element be set for primary keys and non-key fields?
A: Show answer
The chapter directs that a field with Key Type set to Primary should have Uniqueness set to Unique. Other fields are typically set to Non-Unique, but the designer must consider how a non-key field’s values will be used. A non-key may legitimately require unique values under a particular business assumption, such as an employee identifier used to manage only one department at a time. The setting is therefore not determined by key type alone for all fields. It should reflect the expected meaning and rules of the attribute. The designer should also avoid confusing specification type “Unique” with the separate Uniqueness element that describes stored values.

Study instruction:
- Set Uniqueness for a primary key, a general descriptive field, and a non-key field subject to a genuine uniqueness rule, explaining each decision.

Key point:
- Primary-key values must be Unique.
- Non-key uniqueness depends on the meaning and business use of the field.
35. Q: What does Null Support mean?
A: Show answer
Null Support indicates whether a field can contain a Null value. The chapter recommends “No Nulls” for primary keys and alternate keys and when a value is required. “Nulls Allowed” may be appropriate when the information can legitimately be unknown or unavailable at the time the record is created, such as a customer’s county when the customer has not provided it. Null is not the same as a blank or a meaningful value like “None” or “Not Applicable.” If such labels are legitimate values for the field, they should be explicitly identified in its Range of Values rather than represented by a Null or an empty entry.

Study instruction:
- For a range of fields, decide whether Null is legitimate and distinguish unknown or missing values from meaningful business terms such as “Not Applicable.”

Key point:
- Null represents an absent or unknown value, not a blank or an ordinary business value.
- Use Nulls only when there is a valid reason for the field to permit them.
36. Q: What is the difference between a Null value, a blank value, and a meaningful value such as “None”?
A: Show answer
A Null indicates that a value is missing or unknown. A blank is an empty input and should not be used as a substitute for a meaningful business value. Terms such as “None,” “Not Applicable,” “No Response,” or “Not Wanted” may each represent a valid, deliberate state, depending on the field’s purpose. When one of these terms is meaningful, it should be included as an explicit valid value in the Range of Values. Treating all these states as Null or blank removes important distinctions and can make reporting and data interpretation unreliable. The data dictionary should clearly identify which states are permitted and how they are represented.

Study instruction:
- Define the difference between unknown, not applicable, none, and intentionally blank for one business field and specify how each should be recorded.

Key point:
- Null means missing or unknown; it is not a general-purpose substitute for other states.
- Meaningful alternatives should be explicit valid values, not blanks.
37. Q: What does the Values Entered By element specify?
A: Show answer
Values Entered By identifies whether a field’s values are supplied by a user or by the system. “User” means that a person enters the value manually. “System” means that the database application provides it automatically, but only if the application has been designed with a mechanism to generate that value. The distinction helps clarify responsibility for supplying data and informs later implementation of data-entry procedures. It should not be assumed that a value is system-generated simply because automation would be convenient; the implementation must actually provide a controlled way to produce the value.

Study instruction:
- Classify fields in a sample database as user-entered or system-entered and explain what application mechanism would be needed for each system-generated value.

Key point:
- Values Entered By documents the origin of the field’s value.
- System entry must be supported by an actual generation process in the application.
38. Q: What does the Required Value element control?
A: Show answer
Required Value indicates whether a user must supply a value for a field. The chapter notes that many fields may not need to be mandatory, but a primary-key field must have Required Value set to Yes. Other fields may also be required where the business process cannot function without the information. For example, a postal code may be necessary for delivering a letter or package to a customer. This element is related to, but not identical with, Null Support: Required Value describes whether entry is required, while Null Support records whether Null is allowed. The settings should be coordinated so that the specification is internally consistent.

Study instruction:
- Identify mandatory attributes in a business process and set Required Value based on operational need, then check that Null Support agrees with the decision.

Key point:
- Required Value determines whether information must be supplied.
- Primary keys must be required, and other fields may be required by business needs.
39. Q: How are Required Value and Null Support related, and how are they different?
A: Show answer
Both elements concern whether a field may lack a value, but they express different aspects of the specification. Required Value records whether users are obliged to supply information, while Null Support states whether the field can accept Null. The chapter recommends No Nulls when a value is required and uses No Nulls for primary and alternate keys. If a field is optional at record creation, the designer must still decide whether a Null is legitimate and whether the user is expected to enter the value later. The two settings should not contradict one another; the field specification must describe a coherent rule for missing information and the timing of its entry.

Study instruction:
- Prepare examples for mandatory, optional-but-later-required, and genuinely unknown fields and specify Required Value and Null Support consistently for each.

Key point:
- Required Value addresses obligation to enter; Null Support addresses acceptance of Null.
- Review both settings together to prevent conflicting specifications.
40. Q: What is the Range of Values element?
A: Show answer
Range of Values specifies all valid values that may be stored in a field. It can be expressed through a numeric lower and upper limit or as a defined list of accepted values. The chapter groups ranges into General, Integrity-specific, and Business-specific categories. During this stage of design, the focus is on the General range: the complete set of values generally valid for the field. Integrity-specific values depend on a field’s role in a table relationship, while Business-specific values arise from organizational requirements and business rules. These additional restrictions are revisited in later design stages, so the designer should distinguish the general definition from rules that depend on relationships or organizational policy.

Study instruction:
- Define a general range for a field using either a list or boundaries, then identify any separate restrictions that depend on relationships or business rules.

Key point:
- Range of Values defines the valid value set for a field.
- General, integrity-specific, and business-specific restrictions are distinct categories.
41. Q: What is the difference between General, Integrity-specific, and Business-specific ranges of values?
A: Show answer
A General range describes the complete collection of values ordinarily valid for the field, such as recognized state abbreviations. An Integrity-specific range is determined by the field’s role within a table relationship and is addressed when relationships are designed. A Business-specific range is determined by an organization’s requirements, such as limiting a state field to locations in which the business operates. At this stage, the designer establishes the General range and revisits the other categories when the relevant relationship and business-rule work is performed. Keeping the categories separate prevents a temporary organizational limitation from being mistaken for the universal meaning of a field.

Study instruction:
- Classify sample restrictions as General, Integrity-specific, or Business-specific and identify at which design stage each should be finalized.

Key point:
- General describes valid values broadly; integrity and business ranges add context-specific limits.
- Do not prematurely treat later-stage relationship or business rules as general field meaning.
42. Q: Why should “Other” and “Miscellaneous” generally be excluded from a field’s Range of Values?
A: Show answer
These terms do not identify specific, meaningful values and can conceal an incomplete understanding of the field. If users select “Other” or “Miscellaneous,” the database may record that an item does not fit a known category without capturing what the item actually is. The presence of such values may indicate that the field needs further refinement or that the range has not been properly investigated. The designer should determine which values are legitimately valid and specify them clearly. If an open-ended response is truly required, the design should provide a meaningful method to capture the detail rather than relying on a vague catch-all category.

Study instruction:
- Review a list of permitted values containing “Other” or “Miscellaneous” and determine what additional categories or data-capture requirements are needed to make the range meaningful.

Key point:
- Catch-all values can obscure incomplete analysis and reduce data usefulness.
- Define specific valid values rather than relying on vague placeholders.
43. Q: What is an Edit Rule?
A: Show answer
Edit Rule specifies when a user may enter a field value and whether the value can be modified afterward. It combines the timing of initial entry with the permission to edit the value. The chapter provides four combinations of immediate or later entry and editable or non-editable values, plus an option to leave the decision undetermined until implementation in an RDBMS. The element makes data-entry expectations explicit and helps identify where a value must be captured at record creation, may be supplied later, or must remain unchanged after it has been entered. The selected rule should reflect the business process and any appropriate control requirements.

Study instruction:
- Select an Edit Rule for several fields and explain both when the value must first be supplied and whether subsequent changes are permitted.

Key point:
- Edit Rule controls timing of entry and subsequent modification.
- Immediate/later entry and editable/non-editable status are separate decision dimensions.
44. Q: What does “Enter Now, Edits Allowed” mean?
A: Show answer
The user must enter a value when creating a new record in the field’s parent table, but the value can be edited later. This setting is appropriate when the field is essential at the time the record is created but may legitimately change during the subject’s lifecycle. The setting should not be confused with an optional field or a field that is permanently locked after its first entry. If changes are allowed, the organization may still need approval, audit history, or other controls in the implemented application, depending on the nature of the field. The logical specification defines that edits are permitted; implementation determines how those edits are governed.

Study instruction:
- Identify a field that must be completed at record creation but may change later, and explain why this Edit Rule fits its business purpose.

Key point:
- The value is mandatory at record creation and may later be edited.
- Permission to edit does not remove the need for appropriate change controls.
45. Q: What does “Enter Later, Edits Allowed” mean?
A: Show answer
The user may create the record without entering the value immediately, but the value must be supplied at some point in the near future. Once entered, it can be changed later. This rule does not mean that the field can remain Null indefinitely. The timing allowed for later entry must be determined and enforced when the database is implemented. The setting is suitable for information that may not be available at the moment the record is first created but is expected to be obtained through a subsequent step in the process. The organization should define how the outstanding value is tracked and when it becomes overdue.

Study instruction:
- Design a workflow for a field that may be completed after record creation, specifying who must provide it and how outstanding values will be monitored.

Key point:
- Later entry is a temporary allowance, not a permanent exemption from completion.
- The implementation must establish how the completion deadline is determined and enforced.
46. Q: What does “Enter Now, Edits Not Allowed” mean?
A: Show answer
The user must supply the value when the record is created, and the value cannot be edited afterward. This rule is appropriate where the value must be captured immediately and should remain fixed after entry under the organization’s process. The restriction is stronger than simply marking a field as required: it also limits subsequent changes. The organization should consider whether exceptional corrections could ever be necessary and, if so, how those corrections should be authorized and documented during implementation. The logical rule states that ordinary edits are not allowed; the technical control and exception process must ensure that the restriction is applied consistently.

Study instruction:
- Identify a field whose value should be captured at creation and then locked, and document how a legitimate error correction would be escalated.

Key point:
- Immediate entry is mandatory and subsequent edits are prohibited.
- Any exceptional correction process should be separately controlled and documented.
47. Q: What does “Enter Later, Edits Not Allowed” mean?
A: Show answer
The user may create the record before the value is available, but must enter the value later. Once it has been entered, it cannot be changed. As with the editable version, later entry is not permission to leave the field permanently empty. The implementation must determine the time limit and process for collecting the value. The restriction on editing means that the organization should be especially careful to verify the value at the time it is entered, because ordinary correction will not be permitted afterward. Any necessary exception must be handled under a controlled procedure rather than by casual modification.

Study instruction:
- Create a process for a delayed but immutable field value, including the responsible person, due point, validation, and authorized exception path.

Key point:
- The value can be delayed but must eventually be supplied.
- Once entered, it is not ordinarily editable, making initial validation especially important.
48. Q: When should the Edit Rule be set to “Not Determined At This Time”?
A: Show answer
This option is used when the final edit rule will be decided during implementation in the selected RDBMS. It acknowledges that the logical design stage may not yet have enough information to define the complete technical behavior. The setting should not be used as a substitute for analysis where the business process is already understood. The designer should identify what remains undecided and ensure that the implementation team revisits it before deploying the field. The chapter distinguishes this option from later-entry rules: it is a deferral of the decision itself, not a statement that the user can enter the value later.

Study instruction:
- Identify fields whose edit behavior depends on implementation decisions and document what information is required before the rule can be finalized.

Key point:
- “Not Determined At This Time” defers the edit-rule decision to implementation.
- Unresolved settings should be tracked so they are not accidentally omitted from the final build.
49. Q: What is the difference between the Unique, Generic, and Replica specification types in practical use?
A: Show answer
Unique is used when one specific field needs its own definition or when the field is a primary key. Generic is used when several fields share a general meaning and should begin with consistent, broad settings. Replica is used when a field is based on a Generic specification or serves as a foreign key, drawing most settings from its source while allowing justified adjustments. For example, a generic STATE specification can serve as the basis for VEND STATE, while a vendor-specific Replica can inherit the two-character alphabetic format and adapt its logical settings if needed. The types form a controlled reuse method that reduces inconsistent definitions across the database.

Study instruction:
- Create a Generic State template and two Replica specifications for different parent tables, documenting which settings are inherited and which require adjustment.

Key point:
- The three types provide a consistent method for independent fields, reusable templates, and derived fields.
- Reuse should not erase legitimate differences in individual field requirements.
50. Q: How should a Generic State specification be designed so that it can be reused?
A: Show answer
The specification should use a nonspecific field name such as STATE and describe a state or territory in broad terms. Its physical settings should reflect the general format needed, such as an alphanumeric field of appropriate length with alphabetic character support. Its general range should include the recognized state abbreviations relevant to the intended scope. The Generic specification should omit Parent Table, Shared By, Alias(es), and Source Specification, because those elements are specific to an individual field or replica. It then serves as a template for fields such as customer state, employee state, and vendor state, each of which can be defined separately as a Replica.

Study instruction:
- Draft a reusable State template and check that its name, description, physical settings, logical settings, and excluded elements satisfy the Generic specification rules.

Key point:
- A Generic specification should be broad enough to serve every field with the same general meaning.
- Exclude elements that only make sense for a specific parent field or replica relationship.
51. Q: How should a Replica specification based on a Generic field be adapted for its specific table?
A: Show answer
Begin with the Generic specification and carry over its applicable element settings. Then identify the specific field name and parent table and add any field-specific details not included in the source. If the individual field has requirements that differ from the generic template, adjust the inherited settings so that the Replica accurately represents its actual use. The source specification should be named so that reviewers can trace the origin of the inherited settings. This approach gives fields with the same general meaning a consistent baseline while allowing their individual table context and business needs to be documented correctly.

Study instruction:
- Create a Replica field from a Generic template and document each inherited element, each added element, and every deliberate change.

Key point:
- Replica inherits a baseline but can be tailored to the individual field.
- Record the source and justify any changes rather than silently diverging from the template.
52. Q: Why does a primary-key field usually require specific logical settings in its field specification?
A: Show answer
A primary key must uniquely identify every record and must always be present, so its logical settings should reflect that role. The chapter’s examples set Key Type to Primary, Key Structure to Simple or Composite according to the table design, Uniqueness to Unique, Null Support to No Nulls, and Required Value to Yes. The example also shows system entry and an edit restriction for a generated vendor identifier, but those settings should reflect the actual key-generation process and organizational requirements rather than being assumed for every primary key. The specification must be internally consistent with the primary-key elements established in the preceding chapter.

Study instruction:
- Complete the Logical Elements for a primary-key field and explain which settings are required by its key role and which depend on how the identifier is generated and maintained.

Key point:
- Primary-key fields must be unique, non-Null, and required.
- Entry source and edit behavior should reflect the actual identifier-management process.
53. Q: How can field specifications serve as the database’s data dictionary?
A: Show answer
Every completed field specification records the field’s name, ownership, definition, physical structure, valid values, key role, and modification rules. When these specifications are collected for all fields, they form a dictionary of the database’s structure and meaning. The data dictionary helps designers, users, and implementation teams understand how each field should be created and how its values should be entered and validated. It also provides a baseline for reviewing changes: when a requirement changes, the relevant specification can be assessed for impact rather than relying on undocumented assumptions. The dictionary is therefore both a design deliverable and a reference for implementation and ongoing governance.

Study instruction:
- Assemble several field specifications into a small data dictionary and explain how an implementation developer and a business user would each use it.

Key point:
- The complete set of field specifications is the database data dictionary.
- It supports field creation, validation design, shared understanding, and controlled maintenance.
54. Q: How should a designer define field specifications before meeting with users and management?
A: Show answer
The designer should complete as many specifications as possible using existing requirements, analysis notes, and knowledge of the data. Familiar fields can often be specified without waiting for group discussion. The designer should use sound judgment for initial settings and record areas of uncertainty rather than leaving all work until the meetings. The chapter cautions against trying to define every element in isolation; users and managers may know important facts about business meaning, valid values, and logical requirements that the designer does not. The most efficient approach is to produce a well-prepared draft and then use the review meetings to refine it and complete the remaining specifications.

Study instruction:
- Prepare draft specifications for a set of familiar fields and mark any assumptions or unknown settings to be confirmed with the relevant participants.

Key point:
- Complete what can be established from existing knowledge before interviews.
- Use the meetings to validate assumptions and resolve fields that require business expertise.
55. Q: What should happen at the first field-specification review meeting with users and management?
A: Show answer
Begin by explaining the elements of a field specification so that participants understand what information is being requested and how their input will be used. The explanation should be concise but sufficient to give participants the knowledge needed to review field names, meanings, physical settings, and logical rules. Then review the draft specifications and ask whether the element settings are suitable and correct. Participants may reveal new facts, such as a known set of values used for a field, that require changes to the Range of Values or other settings. Review one specification at a time, refine it based on the discussion, and move on when participants have no further suggestions.

Study instruction:
- Design a short briefing and review agenda that explains each specification category and gathers participant feedback field by field.

Key point:
- Participants need to understand the specification elements before they can review them effectively.
- Review and refine each field systematically, capturing new information as it emerges.
56. Q: How should unresolved or unfamiliar field specifications be completed?
A: Show answer
Work with the people who are most familiar with the fields under discussion, because they are more likely to understand the relevant business rules and logical requirements. Ask them to help determine the appropriate settings and record the decisions on the Field Specifications sheet. It is not necessary for the same group to define every field if responsibility and knowledge differ across the organization. After the remaining fields have been discussed and every specification has been completed, the field-specification stage is finished. Any decisions that depend on later relationship or business-rule stages should be recognized as such and revisited when that work is performed.

Study instruction:
- Map each unresolved field to the staff role most knowledgeable about its use and prepare targeted questions to complete the specification.

Key point:
- Use subject-matter knowledge to resolve specifications that the designer cannot reliably determine alone.
- Complete every field while keeping later-stage decisions clearly identified for follow-up.
57. Q: What does the Product Description example demonstrate about defining field specifications?
A: Show answer
The example shows how the designer can define most of a field’s specification before meeting with users and management. For PRODUCT DESCRIPTION, the field is described in business terms, assigned an Alphanumeric data type and a suitable length, and given character support that permits the types of text expected in a description. Its logical settings specify that it is a non-key, non-unique, non-Null field entered by a user and required for the relevant product record. The example demonstrates that each setting should follow the actual purpose and behavior of the field, rather than using one default specification for every field in the database.

Study instruction:
- Review a descriptive text field and produce a complete specification, justifying the selected data type, length, character support, Null setting, and edit rule.

Key point:
- The physical and logical settings should reflect the field’s actual purpose and expected values.
- A complete example helps reveal whether any specification element has been overlooked.
58. Q: What should a designer do when users cannot provide the complete Range of Values for a field?
A: Show answer
Use the broadest reasonable general range that can be established from the available information, and record the uncertainty rather than inventing a complete list. In the Mike’s Bikes example, staff could not identify every valid product category, so the designer used a general definition covering valid internal or external product categories. The field could then be revisited when the organization’s business rules were defined. This approach allows the design to progress while acknowledging that the full restriction is not yet known. The designer should return to the field at the appropriate later stage and replace the provisional broad range with a validated rule if the business requirements support one.

Study instruction:
- Draft a broad general range for a field whose values are not fully known and identify the information and stakeholder decisions required to finalize it later.

Key point:
- Do not invent a value list when the organization cannot substantiate it.
- Record a defensible general range and revisit business-specific restrictions during the business-rule stage.
59. Q: How do field specifications support the later implementation of an RDBMS and user interface?
A: Show answer
The specifications provide the design information needed to create fields with appropriate data types, lengths, precision, and character restrictions. They also guide validation and data-entry procedures by describing required values, valid ranges, Null handling, uniqueness, and edit behavior. The implementation team can use the data dictionary as a reference when translating the logical settings into the specific features available in the selected RDBMS. Application screens and interface rules can then be designed to help users enter suitable values, but the integrity requirement should not depend solely on the user interface. The underlying database design and enforcement mechanisms should reflect the defined specifications.

Study instruction:
- Select a completed field specification and map each element to a proposed database definition, validation control, or user-interface behavior in a target implementation.

Key point:
- Field specifications bridge logical design and technical implementation.
- Validation should be supported by database controls as well as appropriate user-interface procedures.
60. Q: Why is relying only on careful data-entry staff or a “foolproof” user interface insufficient for data integrity?
A: Show answer
Human attention and interface design are useful safeguards, but neither replaces a complete data model and enforceable field specifications. Users can make mistakes, interfaces can be bypassed or changed, and different applications may enter or update the same data. Without clear rules for field meaning, acceptable values, Nulls, uniqueness, and modification, the database can accumulate inconsistent or invalid values even when staff are conscientious. Field specifications establish the underlying requirements that should guide both the database and any user interface. The organization should design integrity into the structure rather than relying entirely on training or visual prompts to prevent mistakes.

Study instruction:
- Identify ways invalid data could enter a database even when users receive training and the interface includes validation messages, then map each risk to a specification or database-level control.

Key point:
- People and interfaces alone cannot guarantee data integrity.
- Integrity must be designed into the field definitions and consistently enforced.
61. Q: How should the chapter’s field-specification process be governed as requirements change?
A: Show answer
Treat the data dictionary as a controlled design reference and update the affected specification when the meaning, valid values, ownership, or permitted modifications of a field change. A change to a business process may affect the Range of Values, Required Value, Null Support, or Edit Rule, while a change to the database structure may affect Parent Table, Shared By, Key Type, or Specification Type. The organization should identify who owns the definition, who approves changes, and how updated specifications are communicated to implementers and users. These governance practices are practical implications of maintaining a complete specification; the precise approval process depends on the organization’s standards and development arrangements.

Study instruction:
- Create a controlled-change procedure for one field specification, including change rationale, review, approval, versioning, and communication to affected teams.

Key point:
- Field specifications must remain aligned with current business and structural requirements.
- Controlled updates preserve consistency between the data dictionary and implemented database.
62. Q: What are the key lessons from Chapter 9 before proceeding to table relationships?
A: Show answer
Every field needs a complete specification so that its meaning, structure, valid values, and modification rules are clear. The specification is composed of General, Physical, and Logical Elements and can be Unique, Generic, or Replica depending on how the field is used. Descriptions should be plain, concise, and independent, while physical settings should reflect the field’s true data format and logical settings should establish its key role, Null policy, required status, valid values, and edit behavior. Generic and Replica specifications help maintain consistency across related fields. Finally, users and management should review the designer’s draft and help resolve the fields whose business meaning or rules are not yet known. This creates a data dictionary and a foundation for the subsequent relationship-design stage.

Study instruction:
- Prepare a chapter review checklist covering all specification categories, the three specification types, description standards, value controls, and the stakeholder review process.

Key point:
- Complete field specifications establish field-level integrity and create the data dictionary.
- Relationships and business rules will refine some settings further in later design stages.
Rows: 62
Table 10
Table Relationships: Identification, Design, and Integrity
1. Q: Why are relationships a critical part of a relational database?
A: Show answer
Relationships connect tables that represent logically associated subjects, allowing records in one table to be matched with records in another. They make it possible to retrieve meaningful information across tables without copying all related attributes into one structure. Defining relationships also exposes opportunities to refine table structures and reduce duplicate and redundant data. A sound relationship supports reliable inserts, updates, and deletes; an incorrectly defined one can make data entry difficult, create orphaned records, or produce misleading results when information is combined. Relationships are therefore part of the database's integrity design, not merely lines added to a diagram.

Study instruction:
- Use a small example such as customers and orders. Identify what each table represents, how a customer is connected to orders, and which errors could occur if the connection were missing or incorrect.

Key point:
- Relationships connect logically related records and support reliable cross-table information.
- Their design affects redundancy, data operations, and integrity.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 293–295. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
2. Q: What is a table relationship, and which three characteristics must be defined?
A: Show answer
A table relationship is a defined association between records in two tables, or between records within one table in a recursive design. The chapter distinguishes three characteristics: relationship type, type of participation, and degree of participation. Relationship type describes how records on the two sides can be associated, such as one-to-one or one-to-many. Participation states whether records must exist on a side before related records can be entered. Degree specifies the minimum and maximum number of related records permitted for each record. These characteristics answer different questions and should not be treated as interchangeable.

Study instruction:
- For a customer-to-order relationship, write one sentence describing its type, decide whether a customer may exist before an order, and state the permitted number of orders per customer.

Key point:
- Type, participation, and degree describe different aspects of a relationship.
- A complete design addresses all three.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 293–296, 348–360. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
3. Q: What are the three principal types of relationships between two tables?
A: Show answer
The three types are one-to-one (1:1), one-to-many (1:N), and many-to-many (M:N). In a 1:1 relationship, each record on either side is associated with no more than one record on the other side, subject to the participation rules. In a 1:N relationship, one record on the first side can be associated with multiple records on the second side, while each record on the second side relates to one record on the first. In an M:N relationship, records on both sides can be associated with multiple records on the opposite side. The type is determined from the business meaning of the records, not simply from the current sample data.

Study instruction:
- Classify employee and compensation, customer and orders, and student and classes. Explain the permitted associations in both directions before assigning a symbol.

Key point:
- The three types are 1:1, 1:N, and M:N.
- Determine cardinality from the real-world rules, not from a small sample alone.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 295–303. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
4. Q: When is a one-to-one relationship appropriate?
A: Show answer
A one-to-one relationship is appropriate when one record in each table can be associated with only one record in the other table. It may separate information with different access, security, lifecycle, or organizational purposes, as in the chapter's EMPLOYEES and COMPENSATION example. It can also occur between a parent data table and a subset table. The split should have a defensible design reason; separating columns without a meaningful distinction adds joins and administration without necessarily improving the model. In a typical 1:1 implementation, the child table's foreign key is unique and often also serves as its primary key.

Study instruction:
- For a proposed 1:1 split, document why the attributes belong in separate tables and verify that the rule is truly one record to one record in both directions.

Key point:
- Use 1:1 only when the domain rule genuinely limits each side to one related record.
- Security or subset-table structure can justify a split.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 296–298, 323–327. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
5. Q: How does a one-to-many relationship work, and why is it common?
A: Show answer
A one-to-many relationship allows one record in the parent or one-side table to relate to multiple records in the child or many-side table, while each child record relates to one parent record. The chapter's CUSTOMERS and CUSTOMER RENTALS example illustrates this: one customer can have several rental records, while each rental record is associated with one customer at a given time. This pattern is common because many business events or details belong to one relatively stable subject. It avoids repeating the parent's descriptive attributes in every child record and provides a straightforward location for the foreign key.

Study instruction:
- Choose a parent entity and its event or detail records. Confirm that each child has one parent and that one parent can have several children.

Key point:
- A 1:N relationship places the foreign key on the many side.
- It is a common way to reduce repeated descriptive data.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 298–301. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
6. Q: What defines a many-to-many relationship?
A: Show answer
A many-to-many relationship exists when a record in the first table can be associated with multiple records in the second table and a record in the second table can also be associated with multiple records in the first. Students and classes are the chapter's example: a student may attend several classes, and a class may have several students. The relationship is a statement about the business domain. It does not mean that every student attends every class, nor that every possible pair must exist. Each actual association is a separate fact that must be represented in the design.

Study instruction:
- Write the rule from both perspectives: one student to how many classes, and one class to how many students. Then identify what data records each actual enrollment.

Key point:
- M:N permits multiple associations in both directions.
- Each actual pairing is a meaningful association, not an assumed universal match.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 301–304. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
7. Q: What problems arise when a many-to-many relationship is left without a proper linking structure?
A: Show answer
Without a proper linking structure, the database has no clean way to record each association. Attempts to place repeated foreign-key columns in one table create a fixed number of slots and effectively introduce a multivalued field. Repeating complete rows to represent each pairing duplicates parent attributes and creates redundancy. These designs make insertion difficult when one side has no related record, can make deletion remove the only copy of a subject's details, and complicate updates because the same facts may need to be changed in several rows. Retrieving data also becomes cumbersome because the association is not represented as a consistent set of records.

Study instruction:
- Take a student with several enrollments and sketch both an array-of-Student-ID design and a flattened repeated-row design. Identify insertion, update, and deletion problems in each.

Key point:
- Unresolved M:N relationships encourage repeating groups and duplicated facts.
- The resulting structure weakens data maintenance and integrity.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 304–308. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
8. Q: Why is adding Student ID 1, Student ID 2, and similar columns not a sound solution to an M:N relationship?
A: Show answer
A set of numbered columns imposes an arbitrary maximum number of related students and leaves unused columns for classes with fewer students. It also makes searching, validating, and adding a relationship dependent on which slot is used. Increasing the maximum requires structural changes, while a class with no student may have no meaningful values for the repeated fields. The design is a flattened multivalued field rather than a normalized representation of the associations. The same defect occurs if a fixed number of Class ID columns is added to STUDENTS instead.

Study instruction:
- Explain how the proposed structure behaves when a class has one student, many students, or more students than the available columns. Identify why adding another column is not a scalable data-model solution.

Key point:
- Repeated numbered columns encode a collection inside one row.
- A variable number of associations should be represented as rows in a related table.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 304–307. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
9. Q: How does a linking table resolve a many-to-many relationship?
A: Show answer
A linking table represents each association as its own record. The designer copies the primary key from each of the two parent tables into the linking table. Each copied field is a foreign key to its respective parent, and together the fields normally form a composite primary key. The original M:N relationship is thereby replaced by two 1:N relationships: one from the first parent to the linking table and one from the second parent to the linking table. The linking table is named to describe the association, such as STUDENT CLASSES for students enrolled in classes.

Study instruction:
- Draw STUDENTS, CLASSES, and STUDENT CLASSES. Mark both foreign keys, draw the two 1:N relationships, and show how one student can have multiple linking rows.

Key point:
- A linking table converts one M:N relationship into two 1:N relationships.
- Each row records one association between parent records.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 331–333. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
10. Q: Why does a linking table normally use a composite primary key?
A: Show answer
The copied parent keys together identify the particular pair of records represented by a linking row. In STUDENT CLASSES, Student ID plus Class ID prevents the same student-class pairing from being entered twice when a student may enroll in a class only once under the modeled conditions. The chapter describes this composite key as the normal logical-design approach, while acknowledging that physical design may sometimes use a different key. If a surrogate key is introduced physically, the design still needs a uniqueness rule for the natural association where duplicate pairings are not allowed. Additional attributes may be needed in the composite key when the same pair can validly recur in different contexts.

Study instruction:
- For a linking table, state what makes one association unique. Test whether the parent-key pair is sufficient or whether a term, version, date, or other discriminator is required.

Key point:
- The parent-key pair normally forms the linking table's logical composite key.
- Any physical alternative must still prevent invalid duplicate associations.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 331–333. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
11. Q: When should a linking table contain attributes beyond its two foreign keys?
A: Show answer
A linking table should contain attributes that describe the association itself rather than either parent subject independently. In the chapter's ORDER DETAILS example, Quantity Ordered and Quote Price depend on a particular product as included in a particular order. They therefore belong with the Order Number and Product Number in ORDER DETAILS, not in ORDERS or PRODUCTS. Likewise, Term may be needed in a student-class association if the same student can take the same class in different terms. Locating these attributes in the linking table avoids repeating values at the wrong level and aligns each fact with the key that identifies it.

Study instruction:
- For each attribute proposed for a linking table, ask whether its value is determined by the first parent, the second parent, or the specific pairing. Place association-dependent facts with the pairing.

Key point:
- Attributes describing a pairing belong in the linking table.
- Their placement should match the key that identifies the association.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 333–337. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
12. Q: What is a self-referencing or recursive relationship?
A: Show answer
A self-referencing relationship connects records within the same table rather than connecting two distinct tables. A record is associated with one or more other records that represent the same kind of subject. The chapter gives examples such as members sponsoring members, employees managing employees, customers referring customers, and parts containing other parts. A self-referencing relationship can be 1:1, 1:N, or M:N. It is still treated as a table relationship during design, but the key that establishes the association refers back to the primary key in the same table.

Study instruction:
- Identify a table in which one instance of the subject can be related to another instance of that same subject. State the role played by each record in the association.

Key point:
- A recursive relationship links records within one table.
- It can have any of the three principal relationship types.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 308–312. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
13. Q: How is a self-referencing one-to-one relationship represented?
A: Show answer
A self-referencing 1:1 relationship uses a foreign-key field in the table that draws its values from the table's own primary key. The chapter's MEMBERS example uses Sponsor ID to identify the member who sponsors another member. Under the stated business rule, a member can sponsor only one other member. Sponsor ID is therefore designated as a foreign key referencing Member ID. The foreign key needs a distinct field name because both keys occur in the same table. The precise uniqueness and participation rules must reflect the organization's actual sponsorship policy.

Study instruction:
- Create a MEMBERS example with Member ID and Sponsor ID. Mark Sponsor ID as a foreign key and state the business rule that makes the association one-to-one.

Key point:
- A self-referencing 1:1 uses a foreign key that points to the same table's primary key.
- The business rule must support the one-to-one limit.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 309–310, 337–338. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
14. Q: How is a self-referencing one-to-many relationship represented?
A: Show answer
A self-referencing 1:N relationship uses a foreign-key field in the table that refers to the primary key of another row in that same table. In the STAFF example, Manager ID stores the Staff ID of the employee's manager. One manager can be associated with several staff members, while each staff member reports to one manager under the modeled rule. The chapter notes that the one-side of the diagram may point toward the Manager ID role and the many-side toward Staff ID, so the designer must interpret the roles rather than assume the line always points from a primary key to a foreign key in the usual visual direction.

Study instruction:
- Draw a STAFF table with Staff ID and Manager ID. Populate a small reporting hierarchy and trace how several employees can refer to one manager.

Key point:
- A self-referencing 1:N commonly models hierarchies such as employee supervision.
- The foreign key stores another row's primary-key value.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 310, 338–340. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
15. Q: How is a self-referencing many-to-many relationship established?
A: Show answer
A self-referencing M:N relationship uses a linking table whose two foreign keys both reference the same parent table. For the chapter's PARTS example, a part can contain several component parts and can itself be used as a component in other assemblies. PART COMPONENTS therefore contains Part ID and Component ID, both referencing PARTS. The two roles must be clearly distinguished even though they reference the same key. Together they identify the parent-part and component-part pairing. This structure allows a part to appear as an assembly in one row and as a component in another.

Study instruction:
- Create a PARTS table and a PART COMPONENTS linking table. Label the two foreign keys by role and trace a parent assembly to its components and a component back to its assemblies.

Key point:
- A recursive M:N requires two role-specific foreign keys to the same parent table.
- The linking table records each parent-component pairing.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 311–312, 341–342. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
16. Q: When should a self-referencing relationship be reconsidered or redesigned?
A: Show answer
A self-referencing structure is useful when the subject genuinely relates to other instances of itself, but the chapter cautions that it should serve a clear purpose. Difficulty retrieving information or the discovery of additional facts may reveal that the design needs another entity. For example, a STAFF manager relationship may lead the organization to recognize that it also needs to track departments, their attributes, and staff assignments. A separate DEPARTMENT table and a linking structure can then represent those facts more directly. The decision should come from requirements analysis, not from a preference to avoid recursive relationships at all costs.

Study instruction:
- Review a recursive hierarchy and interview users about what they actually need to track. Determine whether the hierarchy alone is sufficient or whether a separate entity and association table are required.

Key point:
- Keep a recursive relationship when it models a genuine requirement.
- Revisit the structure when new subjects or attributes emerge.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 339–342. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
17. Q: How should a designer begin identifying relationships among existing tables?
A: Show answer
The chapter recommends working with representative users and management because they understand how the organization's subjects relate in practice. Start by listing every table across the top of a matrix and again down its left side, using the same order. Examine each relevant pair systematically and record the relationship observed from the perspective of the row table. The matrix is an analysis aid: it helps ensure that pairs are considered consistently and that self-referencing possibilities are not overlooked. Stakeholder input is valuable, but their assumptions should be tested against actual business processes and sample records.

Study instruction:
- Build a square matrix for five tables in a familiar business area. Identify who can explain each subject and who has authority to confirm the business rules.

Key point:
- A table matrix provides a systematic inventory of candidate relationships.
- Users and management help validate the business meaning behind them.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 312–314. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
18. Q: Why should the relationship-identification process focus on direct relationships?
A: Show answer
A direct relationship exists when the two tables have a specific association of their own. An indirect connection through a third table is not a direct relationship between the original pair. The chapter illustrates this with CLASSES and STAFF: a class is taught by a faculty member, and faculty members are drawn from staff, so the path exists through FACULTY rather than through a direct CLASSES-to-STAFF association. Treating every transitive path as a direct relationship can add unnecessary foreign keys and obscure the actual business rule. The matrix should record the associations that exist directly between the represented subjects.

Study instruction:
- Choose three tables connected by a chain. State which pairs have direct business associations and which are connected only through an intermediate table.

Key point:
- Record direct relationships, not every indirect path through the database.
- Model each association at the level where the business rule actually exists.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 313–314. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
19. Q: What is an associative question for identifying a relationship?
A: Show answer
An associative question asks whether a single record in one table can be associated with one or more records in another table. It is phrased in terms of the records represented by the table names and is asked from each side of the proposed relationship. For example, the designer might ask whether one class can be associated with one or more buildings. For a self-referencing test, the question is adapted to ask whether one instance of the subject can be associated with other instances of the same subject. The answer helps establish the relationship type from that perspective.

Study instruction:
- Write an associative question for each direction of a proposed relationship. Avoid embedding assumptions about how many records must exist.

Key point:
- Associative questions test record-to-record association directly.
- Ask them from both perspectives to establish the complete relationship.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 314–315. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
20. Q: What are contextual questions, and how do their two forms differ?
A: Show answer
Contextual questions place the relationship in the real-world activities or ownership structure represented by the tables. Ownership-oriented questions use ideas such as owns, has, is part of, or contains; for example, whether an order can contain multiple products. Action-oriented questions use verbs such as makes, visits, places, teaches, or attends; for example, whether an instructor teaches multiple classes. Both forms help stakeholders explain the association in language familiar to the organization. They can also be adapted to self-referencing relationships by asking whether one instance owns, contains, manages, or acts upon other instances of the same subject.

Study instruction:
- For one pair of tables, write one ownership-oriented and one action-oriented question. Decide which is clearer for the users who must confirm the relationship.

Key point:
- Contextual questions express relationships through business meaning.
- Ownership and action wording can reveal associations that abstract questions miss.

Source links:
- Source: Chapter 10, “Table Relationships,” Database Design for Mere Mortals, 25th Anniversary Edition, pp. 314–315. No external source URL was supplied or consulted.
21. Q: Why must a designer ask about a pair of tables from both perspectives?
A: Show answer
The number of records that one record can relate to may differ depending on which table is considered first. A class may be associated with several buildings, while a building may contain several classes; these answers together determine the relationship. In a 1:N relationship, one side permits multiple related records and the opposite side permits only one. Asking only one directional question leaves the other half of the cardinality unverified and may cause a 1:N relationship to be mistaken for M:N or 1:1. The chapter therefore records both directional answers before determining the official type.

Study instruction:
- For each proposed relationship, complete two sentences: one beginning with a single record from table A and one beginning with a single record from table B. Compare the answers.

Key point:
